opening: One hot spring evening in Moscow, an editor is telling a young poet that Jesus never existed when a polite foreigner sits down beside them and tells the editor how he will die that night. Within hours the prediction has come true, the poet is in a psychiatric clinic, and a professor of black magic has moved into the dead man's apartment with a talking cat. Bulgakov lets the devil loose in 1930s Moscow to find out what its people will do for money, an apartment or love.

structure.title: Chapters 1–6 · A stranger at Patriarch's Ponds
structure.text: An editor and a poet argue about Jesus with a foreigner who claims to have been in Yershalaim when Pontius Pilate judged a prisoner. His story becomes the novel's second thread. When the poet tries to warn Moscow about the stranger, Moscow decides the poet is mad.

structure.title: Chapters 7–12 · Black magic at the Variety
structure.text: The foreigner and his three companions take over a dead man's apartment and the staff of a theater start disappearing. Their show at the Variety gives the Moscow public exactly what it wants, with consequences the audience discovers on the way home.

structure.title: Chapters 13–18 · The master's story
structure.text: In the clinic the poet meets a nameless writer who tells him about his novel on Pilate and the woman he loved. Meanwhile officials, tenants and relatives keep calling at the apartment on Sadovaya Street, each of them with something to gain.

structure.title: Chapters 19–24 · Margarita
structure.text: The woman the master loved is offered a way to learn what became of him. To accept it she must trust a stranger, rub a cream into her skin and agree to serve as hostess at a very unusual party.

structure.title: Chapter 25 – epilogue · Accounts are settled
structure.text: The story of Pilate is carried through the night after the execution, while in Moscow the police close in on the visitors. Both cities approach the same moonlit evening, and the novel brings its two stories together.

people.name: Woland
people.text: He arrives in Moscow claiming to have breakfasted with Kant and stood beside Pilate. He is courteous, curious and well informed, and he seems more interested in observing Muscovites than in corrupting them.

people.name: Koroviev, Behemoth and Azazello
people.text: A jeering former choirmaster in a checked jacket, a huge black cat who walks on his hind legs, and a fanged red-haired enforcer. They do the work their master prefers not to do himself, mostly with a joke.

people.name: Ivan Bezdomny
people.text: He writes bad verse to order and sees something at Patriarch's Ponds that nobody will believe. His time in the clinic gives him an unexpected teacher.

people.name: The master
people.role: Author of a novel about Pilate
people.text: A historian who gave everything to one book and was crushed when the critics attacked an excerpt. He will not give his name, and he has stopped hoping.

people.name: Margarita
people.text: Comfortably married and deeply unhappy, she has heard nothing from the master for months. She is braver than anyone around her expects.

people.name: Pontius Pilate
people.text: A Roman governor with a headache, a dog and a prisoner he would rather not condemn. The question of what he will do, and what it will cost him, runs through the master's novel.

people.name: Yeshua Ha-Notsri
people.text: A poor, gentle man from Gamala who tells Pilate that there are no evil people and that all power is violence. His story differs from the Gospel accounts in many details.

context.title: Moscow around 1930
context.text: The Moscow chapters are set in a city of shared apartments, housing committees, foreign-currency hunts and people who vanish without explanation. Bulgakov rarely names these things directly; his comedy depends on readers recognising them. When an apartment falls vacant, everyone wants it.

passages.quote: only the housing problem has spoiled them

context.title: The novel inside the novel
context.text: Chapters 2, 16, 25 and 26 tell the story of Pilate in Yershalaim. They reach the reader in different ways: as Woland's story, as Ivan's dream and as pages Margarita reads. They are the master's novel, and their solemn style is meant to sound nothing like the Moscow chapters.

passages.quote: Thus did the fifth procurator of Judea, Pontius Pilate, meet the dawn of the fifteenth of Nisan.

context.title: Massolit and Griboyedov's
context.text: Massolit is Bulgakov's invented association of Moscow writers, housed in Griboyedov House with a famous restaurant downstairs. Membership brings holidays, dachas and good dinners. Its members are the people who decide what the master may publish.

passages.quote: how good life was for the lucky members of Massolit

context.title: Bulgakov's names in Yershalaim
context.text: Bulgakov uses unfamiliar forms on purpose: Yershalaim for Jerusalem, Yeshua Ha-Notsri for Jesus of Nazareth, Levi Matvei for Matthew. His account differs from the Gospels in many details, and the strangeness of the names keeps the reader from reading it as a familiar story.

notice.why: Banknotes rain from the ceiling at the Variety and turn into something else afterward, a bribe crawls into a briefcase by itself, and foreign currency turns up in a ventilation shaft. Each trick shows who wanted the money and what they were prepared to do for it.
The Moscow narrator sounds like a gossip, a police report and a fairground barker by turns, and sometimes addresses you directly. His mock-official tone is part of the joke and part of the disguise.

notice.text: Follow the echoes between the two cities.
notice.why: A full moon, a storm, the smell of roses, a man who sells out another for gain: details from Yershalaim keep recurring in Moscow. Noticing them shows how closely Bulgakov binds the master's novel to the world around it.

passages.quote: More than anything in the world the procurator hated the smell of rose oil

notice.text: Notice who is afraid, and of what.
notice.why: Pilate, the theater staff, the tenants and the critics all act out of fear at some point. Yeshua's view of cowardice gives the book its sharpest measure of these choices.

passages.quote: among the human vices he considered cowardice one of the very chief
